<<2:265 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
2:265/q01 Who are the spenders and what do they seek? [ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمْوَٰلَهُمُ ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ · interpretation]
  2:265/q01/p1 They give sincerely in obedience to God to obtain His approval and reward, without display, reproach, or injury. — reasons: Muqatil and al-Tabari exclude reproach and harm; al-Tabari and al-Mawardi include aid to fighters and obedient Muslims. Al-Hasan excludes reputation. Al-Biqa'i excludes worldly motives and reads marḍāt as lasting satisfaction. Tabataba'i explains God's face as His satisfaction with obedience. Ibn Kathir compares the Ramadan report about faith and seeking reward.
2:265/q02 How are ابتغاء and تثبيتا construed grammatically? [ٱبْتِغَآءَ وَتَثْبِيتًۭا · grammar] (turns on: Whether coordinated تثبيتا can name a purpose of giving, and whether its implied object is God's reward.)
  2:265/q02/p1 Both are circumstantial verbal nouns describing the spenders' state. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya argues coordination makes this the sounder parse and rejects making strengthening the purpose of spending; Abu Hayyan reports and disputes Makki's purpose analysis. Ibn Ashur adopts the circumstantial parse.
  2:265/q02/p2 Both are accusatives of purpose, with تثبيتا coordinated to ابتغاء. — reasons: Al-Nahhas, al-Tabrisi and Makki offer the parse; Abu Hayyan allows it if the object of strengthening is God's reward, since securing reward can motivate spending. Ibn Atiyya objects that spending is not undertaken for the sake of being strengthened.
  2:265/q02/p3 The wording admits either purpose or circumstance; ابتغاء alone may be purposeful even if تثبيتا is circumstantial. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya accepts a purpose sense for ابتغاء alone; al-Samin and Abu Hayyan allow both analyses. Al-Qurtubi records both proposals.
2:265/q03 What does تثبيتا من أنفسهم mean? [وَتَثْبِيتًۭا مِّنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ · interpretation] (turns on: The causative force of tathbīt, its implied object and agent, and whether the wording can carry the sense of deliberation.)
  2:265/q03/p1 Inward faith, certainty, and belief in God's promised recompense strengthen their resolve to give. — reasons: Al-Tabari derives causative strengthening from Ibn Rawaha's verse and says the donors trust the promise; al-Zajjaj contrasts the hypocrite. Al-Sha'bi, Qatada, Abu Salih, Ibn Abbas and others transmit certainty. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Nahhas and Tabataba'i dispute alternative constructions.
  2:265/q03/p2 They deliberate over where and to whom to give, and test their motive before proceeding. — reasons: Mujahid and Ata emphasize proper allocation; Hasan gives only when the motive is wholly for God. Al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi defend the sense as making oneself firm. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Nahhas and Abu Hayyan object that deliberation requires tathabbatan or an explicit licensing verb; 73:8 is debated.
  2:265/q03/p3 They train or fortify themselves in obedience by giving up beloved wealth, making virtue habitual. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf says wealth is close to life and discipline restrains desire; giving wealth steadies part of the self and wealth plus life all of it, citing 61:11. Razi cites repeated action forming disposition, 14:27, 13:28, 76:9 and the Abu Bakr report. Bursevi cites Busiri and Rumi. Ibn Ashur stresses difficult practice.
  2:265/q03/p4 The self firmly preserves an already pure intention throughout the act of giving. — reasons: Tabataba'i makes the self both agent and implied object; the sequence excludes show from the outset and subsequent reproach or harm. Abu Hayyan likewise speaks of protecting the gift from corruption.
  2:265/q03/p5 They seek and expect reward for themselves. — reasons: Qatada and Ibn Abbas give this gloss. Al-Tabari objects that the root does not mean seeking reward unless the soul's hope is what strengthens its owner; al-Nahhas likewise calls it unfamiliar.
  2:265/q03/p6 Their giving makes their sincere faith apparent to other believers. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf and Razi invoke Mujahid's tabyīnan variant; Alusi repeats it. The reading describes proof of faith, rather than its internal strengthening.
  2:265/q03/p7 It lessens their sins. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi transmits Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik.
  2:265/q03/p8 They give acknowledging that God watches them. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi reports al-Zajjaj.
  2:265/q03/p9 They give willingly, from generous intention. — reasons: Abu Hayyan reports satisfaction in giving zakat; Ibn Atiyya calls Qatada's generosity gloss close to certainty, and al-Durr transmits intention.
2:265/q04 How does من أنفسهم work? [مِّنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the self is part of what is strengthened, the source of strengthening, or the intended object.)
  2:265/q04/p1 من is partitive: giving wealth commits or steadies part of the self. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf uses the idiom of stirring some energy; 61:11 distinguishes wealth from wealth and life. Al-Biqa'i, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur likewise treat wealth as figuratively part of the self; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin attach min to the verbal noun.
  2:265/q04/p2 من marks source: confirmation or resolve arises from within their own selves. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf contrasts this with partitivity; al-Nasafi, Bursevi and Alusi locate conviction in the heart. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin say the self can be the semantic agent; Tabataba'i makes it both agent and object.
  2:265/q04/p3 من takes the place of ل or marks an object or an adjective of تثبيتا. — reasons: Abu al-Baqa supplies deeds as object and permits min as li; al-Samin also offers an adjectival attachment. Al-Jubba'i takes min as li for training oneself in obedience.
2:265/q05 Who or what is compared with the garden? [وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍۭ · grammar] (turns on: What implied term completes the comparison and whether its elements correspond one by one.)
  2:265/q05/p1 The sincere spending or its standing with God is like the fruitful garden. — reasons: Al-Wahidi supplies an omitted 'spending'; Ibn Atiyya permits that syntax. Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi stress the expenditure's growth or standing. Al-Biqa'i says the named spender implies the owner and the named garden implies the expenditure.
  2:265/q05/p2 The giver is like the garden or its planter, while greater and lesser gifts are like heavy and light rain. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya supplies a planter; al-Kashshaf gives a differentiated matching; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi allow the giver or the expenditure to be the primary term.
  2:265/q05/p3 The likeness is a composite of pure, growing expenditure and the fertile, fruitful garden. — reasons: Al-Alusi describes the common feature as growth with purity; the imagery includes both the soil and either amount of rain.
2:265/q06 What does جنة mean here? [جَنَّةٍۭ · meaning]
  2:265/q06/p1 An orchard or tree-covered garden. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain the root by trees concealing the ground; al-Qurtubi compares jinn and embryo. Al-Farra, al-Mubarrad and others distinguish a palm garden, janna, from a vineyard, firdaws.
2:265/q07 Is the image read as a garden or a grain? [جَنَّةٍۭ · readings] (turns on: A reported alternative word in the comparison.)
  2:265/q07/p1 جنة, a garden. — reasons: The standard wording is retained by the sources recording the variant.
  2:265/q07/p2 حبة, a grain or seed. — reasons: Mujahid, Asim al-Jahdari and al-Jahdari are named for the variant; al-Kashshaf and al-Alusi also report it. Al-Samin relates its comparison to 2:261.
2:265/q08 What does ربوة mean? [بِرَبْوَةٍ · meaning] (turns on: Whether rabā denotes geographical elevation, soil's swelling growth, or a low place.)
  2:265/q08/p1 Raised ground, often level and fertile, above its surroundings or runoff. — reasons: Mujahid and Hasan stress level elevation; Ibn Abbas and Dahhak say rivers do not flow through this garden, though al-Qurtubi notes hills may have water. Al-Yazidi specifies above the watercourse. The root rabā means rise or increase; al-A'sha's poem depicts upland gardens. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi limit the no-rivers detail to this rain-fed setting.
  2:265/q08/p2 Fertile soil that swells and rises after rain, rather than an ordinary hill. — reasons: Razi cites 22:5 and the contrast with sterile stone, objecting that hills lack streams and face wind while hollows flood. Bursevi and Study Quran repeat the growth argument.
  2:265/q08/p3 A low place. — reasons: Al-Suddi's rabāwa is transmitted by Ibn Atiyya and others; Ibn Atiyya calls it awkward, and al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin reject it because the root denotes increase and height.
2:265/q09 How is ربوة read? [بِرَبْوَةٍ · readings] (turns on: Dialectal vowel and added-alif forms, with preference based on prevalence and plural morphology.)
  2:265/q09/p1 With ḍamma on rāʾ, rubwa. — reasons: Widely attributed to the Hijaz, Medina and Iraq; Abu Hatim, Abu Ubayd, Abu al-Hasan, al-Akhfash, al-Tabari and al-Tabrisi prefer it as common or because the plural rubā/rubā supports it. The same variation occurs in 23:50.
  2:265/q09/p2 With fatḥa on rāʾ, rabwa. — reasons: Attributed to Asim and Ibn Amir and to Tamim; Ibn Khalawayh calls both principal forms eloquent dialects.
  2:265/q09/p3 With kasra on rāʾ, ribwa. — reasons: Reported from Ibn Abbas and also Hasan, al-A'mash and Abu Ishaq; al-Tabari rejects it as a recitation.
  2:265/q09/p4 Rabāwa with an added alif and fatḥa. — reasons: Attributed to Abu Ja'far, Abu Abd al-Rahman, Ibn Abbas and Abu Razin, with variants reported in 23:50.
  2:265/q09/p5 Rabāwa with added alif and kasra. — reasons: Attributed to al-Ashhab al-Uqayli; reports vary in spelling.
  2:265/q09/p6 A lengthened form with ḍamma. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this to Ubayy and Asim al-Jahdari.
2:265/q10 Why is the garden placed on a rabwa, and what setting is envisaged? [جَنَّةٍۭ بِرَبْوَةٍ · interpretation] (turns on: Elevation and water's agricultural effects, and whether a named region is intended.)
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<2:265 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>

  2:265/q10/p1 Raised, fertile ground produces especially fine, abundant fruit. — reasons: Al-Tabari invokes richer soil and al-A'sha's upland verse. Al-Biqa'i cites sun and pollinating winds; Bursevi and Alusi cite mild, unstagnant air; al-Baydawi cites cool air. Ibn Atiyya rejects identifying Riyad al-Hazn as the precise setting, explaining Najd and Tihama differ; Abu Hayyan follows.
  2:265/q10/p2 The image is the rain-fed, raised garden familiar in Arabia, with no stream in this instance. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya confines Ibn Abbas's no-rivers description to this garden, citing another raised place with a spring in 23:50; al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan agree the word need not exclude water universally.
  2:265/q10/p3 The fertile raised garden may have flowing water. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi describe level raised land supplied by water; Ibn Kathir reports streams in Ibn Abbas's and Dahhak's descriptions, while al-Qurtubi says a rabwa can have water.
  2:265/q10/p4 The parable's land is Egypt. — reasons: Zayd ibn Aslam says dew supports Egyptian soil and heavy rain doubles its yield. Al-Tha'labi's report instead says rain weakens it, a conflicting detail preserved here.
2:265/q11 What does وابل mean? [وَابِلٌۭ · meaning]
  2:265/q11/p1 A heavy, abundant downpour. — reasons: Al-Akhfash gives paired Arabic verb forms for raining and the adjective mobūla; al-Mawardi cites Adi ibn Zayd's verse; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi describe intense rain.
2:265/q12 What is the syntax of أصابها وابل? [أَصَابَهَا وَابِلٌۭ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the rain clause is descriptive or circumstantial, and whether its antecedent is garden or ground.)
  2:265/q12/p1 It is a second adjective describing the garden. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and al-Samin put lasting location before temporary rainfall; al-Qurtubi says the pronoun points to the raised tract.
  2:265/q12/p2 It describes the rabwa, of which the garden is part. — reasons: Abu al-Baqa gives this alternative; al-Qurtubi takes the pronoun as the elevated ground.
  2:265/q12/p3 It is circumstantial from the garden or the pronoun within its location phrase. — reasons: Abu Hayyan allows a circumstantial clause; al-Samin specifies either the implicit pronoun or the now specified garden, with qad understood in the latter.
2:265/q13 What does آتت أكلها mean and how is آتت construed? [فَـَٔاتَتْ أُكُلَهَا · grammar] (turns on: Whether آتت retains 'gave' with an omitted recipient or means 'produced' with one object.)
  2:265/q13/p1 The garden gives its edible produce, with an implicit owner or people as first object and أكلها as second. — reasons: Al-Samin prefers the ordinary two-object construction and calls the giving metaphorical; Abu Hayyan supplies owner or people. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say the possessive is association, not garden ownership.
  2:265/q13/p2 آتت means produced or brought forth, taking أكلها as its sole object. — reasons: Abu al-Baqa offers this and Bursevi permits it; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin's al-Shaykh object that Arabic does not attest this meaning of آتت.
2:265/q14 What does أكلها mean? [أُكُلَهَا · meaning]
  2:265/q14/p1 Its edible fruit, crop, food or produce. — reasons: Al-Akhfash, al-Tabari and Abu al-Hasan distinguish food from the act of eating; the poet's meal/hunger line and 14:25 support edible produce. Al-Mufaddal broadens akl to what strengthens something, like yarn in a garment; Abu Zayd uses it for a person's livelihood. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain the possessive as association.
2:265/q15 How is أكلها read? [أُكُلَهَا · readings] (turns on: Pronunciation with or without the medial vowel; meaning remains produce.)
  2:265/q15/p1 The light form has sukūn on kāf in the feminine possessive. — reasons: Attributed to Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Abu Amr. Abu Amr differs from the first two for masculine and unpossessed forms; al-Khalawayh says lightening avoids consecutive dammas after suffixing. Qiraat-ER says the sense is unchanged.
  2:265/q15/p2 The heavy form keeps the kāf vowelled, with two ḍammas. — reasons: Attributed to Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i throughout; al-Khalawayh calls it the original form. Both pronunciations name produce.
2:265/q16 How much and how often does ضعفين signify? [ضِعْفَيْنِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the dual counts amount, harvests, or repeated multiplication, and the baseline to which a double is compared.)
  2:265/q16/p1 Twice the ordinary or comparable garden's crop. — reasons: Most interpreters count an amount plus its equal; Ata and Ibn Abbas compare one year here with two elsewhere. Al-Qurtubi prefers twice the fruit of other land over two yearly harvests. The cause is the high ground plus heavy rain.
  2:265/q16/p2 Two harvests in one year. — reasons: Ikrima reports two fruitings; al-Tabrisi specifies six months apart and cites 14:25. Al-Qurtubi prefers a quantity comparison instead.
  2:265/q16/p3 Four times the ordinary crop. — reasons: Al-Biqa'i prefers this: each double is original plus its equal, so two doubles are four. Al-Tabrisi, al-Baydawi, Bursevi and others transmit the reckoning.
  2:265/q16/p4 Three times the ordinary crop. — reasons: Abu Muslim is reported by Abu Hayyan; Taj al-Qurra rejects it as unsupported in Arabic.
  2:265/q16/p5 Repeated or manyfold abundance, without an exact count. — reasons: Abu Hayyan favors repeated multiples to match multiplied good deeds; Ibn Ashur compares the dual to labbayk. Al-Alusi reports this reading.
2:265/q17 What grammatical role does ضعفين have? [ضِعْفَيْنِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether آتت has an omitted recipient and the doubled amount is a state, or the doubled amount is made its object.)
  2:265/q17/p1 It is a circumstantial accusative describing the crop as multiplied. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi and al-Baydawi parse it this way; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin reject treating it as a second object of آتت.
  2:265/q17/p2 It is the second object of آتت. — reasons: Reported as a proposal only; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call it erroneous because the garden's produce is already the object.
2:265/q18 What does طل mean? [طَلٌّۭ · meaning] (turns on: Literal fine rain versus a reported figurative extension to dew.)
  2:265/q18/p1 Light, fine drizzle or gentle rain. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj describes persistent fine rain scarcely making runoff; al-Wahidi gives small drops and related forms; Juwair calls it rakk. Ibn Atiyya calls this common Arabic usage; al-Tabrisi records other lexical uses related to moisture. Al-Biqa'i describes dew as an early stage of rainfall.
  2:265/q18/p2 Dew or nighttime moisture on plants. — reasons: Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others report dew; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call this figurative compared with fine rain. Al-Qummi specifies nighttime dew.
2:265/q19 How does فإن لم يصبها وابل فطل work grammatically? [فَإِن لَّمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌۭ فَطَلٌّۭ · grammar] (turns on: Which constituent is omitted after the conditional, and whether any inversion is necessary.)
  2:265/q19/p1 An omitted verb or predicate completes the condition: if no downpour strikes, drizzle does or suffices. — reasons: Al-Farra and al-Tabari supply kāna or a prior event and cite a poem; al-Wahidi compares a one-or-two-slave example. Al-Mubarrad supplies 'rain is enough'; al-Zajjaj says 'what reaches it is light rain.' Abu Hayyan and al-Samin set out subject/predicate and omitted-verb parses, with Imru al-Qays's line as parallel.
  2:265/q19/p2 The order is inverted, so yielding follows either downpour or drizzle. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report and reject this as unnecessary; ordinary order already conveys the sense.
2:265/q20 What happens if only طل reaches the garden? [فَإِن لَّمْ يُصِبْهَا وَابِلٌۭ فَطَلٌّۭ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether light moisture preserves the same multiplied crop or produces a smaller yet reliable one.)
  2:265/q20/p1 The fertile garden still gives a full or doubled yield; little moisture suffices. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf invokes fertile soil; al-Baghawi says steady light dew can do a downpour's work. Razi and Abu Hayyan offer full-yield possibilities; al-Wahidi and al-Nasafi say the crop remains abundant.
  2:265/q20/p2 The garden yields less than under heavy rain, but still yields something beneficial. — reasons: Al-Mawardi argues dew-fed crops are weaker than rain-fed crops; Razi allows this alternative; Ibn Ashur links varying yield to varying sincerity.
2:265/q21 What does the orchard teach about sincere giving? [* · interpretation]
  2:265/q21/p1 Sincere charity or a believer's deed remains fruitful and multiplied, whether the gift is large or small. — reasons: Qatada says God's promise never fails; al-Suddi connects doubled fruit to doubled reward. Al-Mawardi urges giving even a little. Razi, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur say degree depends on sincerity, effort, attachment to wealth, recipient need and accompanying circumstances. Al-Qummi's lawful-date report and al-Qurtubi's Abu Hurayra report depict God nurturing a date to mountain size.
2:265/q22 What does God's seeing deeds convey? [وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ · interpretation]
  2:265/q22/p1 God knows outward deeds and inward motives, records and recompenses them; the close promises reward and warns against display. — reasons: Al-Tabari distinguishes sincere from hurtful giving and warns against neglected obligations; Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and others see both promise and warning. Razi notes amount and manner; al-Biqa'i urges improvement of inward and outward work. Al-Khattabi says basir's form functions as an active participle.
2:265/q23 How is تعملون read, and whom does it address? [تَعْمَلُونَ · readings] (turns on: A change in grammatical person and the antecedent of the third-person pronoun.)
  2:265/q23/p1 Second-person تعملون addresses the audience directly. — reasons: The majority reading shifts from third-person narration to direct address, making God's knowledge a promise and warning.
  2:265/q23/p2 Third-person يعملون

 refers to all people or specifically the donors; one report also relates it to hypocrites. — reasons: Al-Zuhri is named for the variant. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi say a donor-only reference makes it pure promise; Abu Hayyan also mentions hypocrites.
2:265/q24 How does the verse connect with the surrounding spending parables and passage? [* · links] (turns on: Which earlier image supplies the main comparison: the barren rock or the multiplying seed.)
  2:265/q24/p1 It contrasts accepted, fertile giving with showy or harmful giving that the preceding rock image leaves barren. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan contrast 2:264; Ibn Ashur says contrast clarifies rank and renews praise. Al-Tabataba'i treats the linked verses as a unit addressing purpose, manner, good wealth, needy recipients and reward.
  2:265/q24/p2 It develops the earlier seed image: the lasting orchard pictures sustained generosity and further multiplication. — reasons: Al-Biqa'i says the grain represents spending in God's path while the orchard covers every good path. Ibn Ashur says the simpler seed image quickly pictures multiplication; this one has several favorable features. Elmalili says double does not reduce the earlier seven-hundredfold promise.
2:265/q25 What inward lesson is drawn from the garden and rain? [* · inward] (turns on: The image's inward analogue: a lasting disposition of generosity or purification of intention.)
  2:265/q25/p1 Giving fixes generosity in the soul; the ridge signifies higher rank, and stronger or weaker rain signifies different shares of mercy. — reasons: Al-Qashani contrasts the enduring orchard with a grain to express an acquired lasting quality; he calls generosity a divine attribute.
  2:265/q25/p2 Sincere devotion removes hidden idolatry and makes deeds grow; insincere work cannot produce good fruit. — reasons: Bursevi cites Sa'di's thorns-and-flowers analogy, and says pure work seeks no praise. He also assigns symbolic meanings to charity's three letters.
2:265/q26 What reports about charity's effects are cited with this verse? [* · reports] (turns on: Different transmitted statements about charity's effect.)
  2:265/q26/p1 A lawfully earned date given in charity is nurtured by God until it becomes mountain-sized. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites Abu Hurayra's Prophetic report through Muslim and the Muwatta; Study Quran also invokes it.
  2:265/q26/p2 Charity itself speaks of five benefits: growth, enlargement, turning an enemy friendly, preservation and protection. — reasons: Bursevi transmits the report through Ali from the Prophet.
  2:265/q26/p3 Hell prostrates in gratitude when a believer gives charity, because it frees someone from punishment. — reasons: Bursevi reports Makhul's saying.
2:265/q27 How do other cited verses about riba and giving relate to this verse's reward contrast? [* · links]
  2:265/q27/p1 Gift-riba seeking a larger return earns no divine reward, unlike sincere charity; prohibited exchange-riba is distinct. — reasons: Al-Farisi distinguishes unlawful excess in like weighed or measured goods from disliked gift-riba, citing 2:278 and 30:39. He gives conditional and relative parses of 30:39, its omitted resumptive and shift of person, and discusses 74:6: Ikrima forbids seeking more back, while al-Farisi says a jussive parse lacks semantic fit.
2:265/q28 What adjacent grammatical example is discussed alongside this verse? [* · links]
  2:265/q28/p1 In the bird passage, فصرهن can mean cut them or incline them, with different attachments of إليك. — reasons: Al-Farisi records both interpretations of 2:260; Sibawayh attaches إليك to the nearer turning verb, while attachment to خذ also permits an implied later object.
2:265/q29 What do ابتغاء and مرضات mean? [ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ · meaning]
  2:265/q29/p1 ابتغاء means seeking, and مرضات names satisfaction or approval. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi derives marḍāt as the verbal noun of raḍiya.
2:265/q30 What verbal sense underlies تثبيتا? [وَتَثْبِيتًۭا · grammar]
  2:265/q30/p1 Causative ثبّت means to make firm or establish, distinct from intransitive ثبت, to become firm. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and al-Samin's al-Shaykh insist on this distinction, opposing replacement by the intransitive verbal noun unless a licensing verb precedes it.
